blocks.c: Chapter Fifteen: Ysolde Kerrin

She was in the bell-house, of course, because where else would she be, and she was cleaning the sound-bow with a rag and a paste of chalk and oil, exactly as Roake did on the Gull, exactly as Roake had taught Sol to do, and the sight of the same four motions performed by a stranger's hands made the whole eleven years fold up like a chart.

Ysolde Kerrin was seventy-one. She was tall, and had been taller. She wore a bell-master's leather over a miner's coat, and when she turned round she looked at the four of them and did not look surprised, and Sol thought: she has been rehearsing this for eleven years and she is about to be very good at it, and I must not let that count for anything.
"Tamsin," said Kerrin.
"Ysolde."
"You look well."
"I look sixty. You look older than the hills and you're cleaning that bow wrong; you always did. You go with the grain of the metal, not across it."
Kerrin's face broke into a smile so genuine that Sol felt an unwilling tug of liking, and hated it.
"There," said the old woman. "That's my girl. Twenty-two years and the first thing out of her mouth is a correction." She put down the rag. "Who are the others?"
"Company observer," said Sallow, "and I'd be glad if you'd all stop saying that as if it were a disease."
"Frames," said Dov.
"Third-watch hand," said Sol.
Kerrin looked at her for a moment longer than at the others.
"You're the ear," she said.
"How do you know that?"

"Because you came in and looked at the bell before you looked at me, and because you've got your head tipped four degrees to the left, which is what a hand does when she's listening to a room." Kerrin picked up her rag again. "Also because a man in a good coat has been sending me letters about you for a month."
Every head in the bell-house turned.
Sallow, to his credit, did not attempt to look innocent. He took his hat off and turned it round in his hands.
"Well," he said. "Yes."
The story took an hour and Kerrin told it standing up, which Sol came to understand was a kind of courtesy: she was not going to make it comfortable for herself.
The platform was cut loose in seventy-eight. The notice went up in Fourthmonth. Eleven shillings a ticket, and no credit, and no exceptions, and a Company agent at the head of the lift to check them.

"Two hundred and forty stayed," said Kerrin. "Not out of heroism. Out of arithmetic. A man with four children and no shillings cannot buy five tickets, and he will not buy one, and so he does not buy any, and the Company writes down nil."

Lowspire had lasted eleven months on the carry left in its frame. It had gone down eleven feet in the first four, and then more slowly, because the platform's own engineer, a man called Beck, had worked out that if you stopped every hammer and every cart and every source of vibration on the whole structure, the carry drained slower.
"Eleven months of a town on tiptoe," said Kerrin. "The children learned to walk quietly before they learned to run. Then Beck died and I came down."
"With a bell," said Roake.

"With a bell that was sitting in a locked cupboard on a ship, doing nothing, made from the same melt as one being rung four times a day, four beats flat, by a woman I had trained myself and who I knew would go on ringing it four beats flat for the rest of her life." Kerrin's chin came up. "Yes. With a bell. And I have rung it true, twice a day, every day, for eleven years, and I have taken about one part in a hundred of the Meridian Gull's carry, and with it I have held two hundred and eleven people in the air."
"Two hundred and forty," said Sol.
"Two hundred and forty stayed," said Ysolde Kerrin. "Two hundred and eleven are here. I said the first eleven months were slow. I did not say they were kind."
Nobody spoke for a while. Outside the bell-house a dog barked, and someone shushed it, out of a habit eleven years old.
"You could have asked," said Roake, at last, and her voice cracked straight down the middle. "Ysolde. You could have come up that lift and stood on the wharf and asked me."
"Asked you for what, Tamsin? For a part in a hundred? You didn't have it to give. It isn't yours; it's the Company's, and the Company had already written nil in a book."
"You could have asked me."

"Yes," said Kerrin. "And you would have said yes, and they would have taken your papers, and then you would have been a woman with no papers standing on a wharf, and there would be two hundred and eleven fewer people in the world." She turned back to her bell. "I did not steal your carry, girl. I stole your choice. That is the part I would give back if I could, and I can't, and I have not lost a night's sleep over it, and you may make of that what you like."
Sol had promised herself she would keep out of it. She lasted nine more seconds.
"You took it off four ships," she said.
Kerrin's rag stopped.
"Say that again."

"Four ships. The fleet's coal went up four per cent the year after the Gull's refit and it never came back down. Only ours shows in a tally, because only ours is paired, but the carry over this stretch of the Cloudsea has been thin for eleven years and everybody's been paying for it in coal and calling it the price of the season." Sol's heart was going hard. "You didn't steal from a Company, ma'am. You stole from four crews who ring four flat because nobody ever told them any different, and every one of them has been quietly worse at their job for eleven years and doesn't know why."
The bell-house was very quiet.
"Yes," said Ysolde Kerrin at last. "That is true, and I did not know it, and I should have. Write it down."
"Ma'am?"

"You heard me. Get a pen and write it down and put it in your tally, in the margin, in your own hand, so that when they come to make the case there is a line in a book that says the bell-master of Lowspire was told a thing she had not accounted for and did not argue." She turned back to the bow, and her voice, for the first time, was old. "I have kept a very careful book for eleven years, girl. It is the only thing I have left that is honest. Do not let me spoil it now by being proud in front of a child."
